hints: Look at the numbers of carbons first. Cellulose is made from glucose, so ask yourself, is glucose a 5-carbon or a 6-carbon sugar?
Remember that joining monomers by condensation removes one water ($H_2O$) per link, so the polymer repeat unit cannot be identical to free glucose ($C_6H_{12}O_6$).
walkthrough:
**Start with the monomer**

Cellulose is a polysaccharide made only from beta-glucose. Free glucose is a hexose sugar with the formula:
$$C_6H_{12}O_6$$

**Apply condensation**

When two glucose molecules join by a glycosidic bond, one molecule of water ($H_2O$) is removed. So subtract $H_2O$ from glucose:
$$C_6H_{12}O_6 - H_2O = C_6H_{10}O_5$$

**Make it a long polymer**

Cellulose has thousands of glucose units, so we write the repeat unit with an $n$ for number of units:
$$n(C_6H_{12}O_6) \rightarrow (C_6H_{10}O_5)_n + nH_2O$$
That gives the general formula $(C_6H_{10}O_5)_n$.

options.A: This has only 5 carbons, which would suggest a pentose polymer, but cellulose is built from 6-carbon glucose.
options.B: This also has only 5 carbons and too much oxygen, it does not match a polymer of hexose glucose minus water.
options.C: Correct. This is glucose ($C_6H_{12}O_6$) minus $H_2O$ lost in condensation, repeated $n$ times for a polysaccharide.
options.D: This is the formula for a single free glucose monomer, it forgets that water is lost when monomers join to form cellulose.
